title: Making plans together
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: hal turīd an nadhhab ilā + al- + N?

rules.text: An invitation is an + a verb, and both are already yours: an from M3 of the level below, nadhhab from M4. The delta is the person — you ask with YOU and answer with WE, which is the shape every Arabic invitation takes.

The clock takes ORDINALS in the feminine, agreeing with as-sāʿa: as-sāʿa ath-thāniya, ar-rābiʿa, al-khāmisa. M8 of the level below taught cardinals and their gender polarity; this is a different set of words.
The half and the quarter join with wa: wa an-niṣf, wa ar-rubʿ. Both nouns take al-, and both articles assimilate, because n and r are sun letters.

This module is the course's densest run of sun letters — as-sāʿa, ath-thāniya, an-niṣf, ar-rubʿ, as-sabt. The assimilation is SPELLING here, not just sound: the build reads al-sāʿa and as-sāʿa as two different words.
in shāʾ allāh (M6 of the level below) marks a future. In speech it is also how a soft no is given, so a plan sealed only with in shāʾ allāh is not sealed.

sentences.display: hal turīd an nadhhab ilā as-sūq?
sentences.script: هل تريد أن نذهب إلى السوق؟
sentences.cue: Would you like us to go to the market?
sentences.literal: Question want(you-m) that we-go to the-market?

words.note: M4's row from the level below, and the na- prefix is "we". Asking with turīd and answering with nadhhab is the shape of every Arabic invitation.

sentences.trap: Not one new word in the whole sentence. The invitation is a rearrangement of things the learner has had for two levels, which is worth noticing rather than hurrying past.
sentences.sound: NADH-hab, with the dh of "this" and the stress at the front.

variations.display: hal turīdīn an nadhhab ilā al-maṭʿam?
variations.script: هل تريدين أن نذهب إلى المطعم؟
variations.cue: Would you like us to go to the restaurant?
variations.changed: the feminine, visible in both lines

variations.display: hal turīd an nadhhab ilā al-madrasa?
variations.script: هل تريد أن نذهب إلى المدرسة؟
variations.cue: Would you like us to go to the school?
variations.changed: another destination after an

variations.cue: I'd like us to go to the market
variations.changed: said as a wish rather than asked as a question

mistake.why: an is obligatory between two verbs, exactly as M3 of the level below taught. Two verbs never touch.

sentences.usage: The everyday invitation. Asking about "we" rather than "you" is what makes it an invitation and not a question about their plans.
sentences.mnemonic: Ask with you, plan with we.

sentences.cue: Why don't we go to the restaurant?

words.note: M9's row from the level below, doing a job it has never done: with lā after it, it stops asking for a reason and starts making a suggestion.

sentences.trap: It looks like a question about causes and it is an invitation. English does exactly the same thing with "why don't we", so the shape transfers — but the words are all old ones.
sentences.sound: li-MĀ-dhā, with two long ā sounds and the stress on the first.

variations.cue: Why don't we go to the market?
variations.changed: another destination in the same frame

variations.cue: Why don't you come with me?
variations.changed: you instead of we, which turns it back into a real question

variations.cue: Why don't we go tomorrow?
variations.changed: a time from M6 of the level below

mistake.why: lam is a past negative and belongs to a later level. The suggestion takes lā.

sentences.usage: Warmer than S01, because it half-assumes the answer. Among friends it is the commoner of the two.
sentences.mnemonic: A question about reasons, doing the work of an invitation.

words.note: Feminine, which is why every clock ordinal after it is feminine too. s is a sun letter, so the article assimilates and the s is held long.
An ORDINAL, not the cardinal khamsa M8 of the level below taught. Telling the time uses a different set of words, and this is the first of them.

sentences.trap: khamsa is five and al-khāmisa is the fifth. The clock never uses the cardinal, so the numbers a learner already has do not help here.
sentences.sound: as-SĀ-ʿa al-KHĀ-mi-sa — the ʿayn in the middle of the first word is a letter, and the kh opens the second.

variations.cue: We'll go at two o'clock
variations.changed: a different ordinal, and a different sun letter

variations.cue: We'll go at four o'clock
variations.changed: another ordinal, and another sun letter

variations.cue: Shall we go at four o'clock?
variations.changed: asked as a question, with another ordinal

mistake.why: The clock takes an ordinal with al-: as-sāʿa al-khāmisa. The cardinal counts things, not hours.

sentences.usage: How a time is fixed. The whole module turns on this frame and the two that follow it.
sentences.mnemonic: Five counts; the fifth tells the time.

words.note: The ordinal for two. th is a sun letter, so al- assimilates: ath-thāniya, and the th is held long.
A noun, joined to the hour with wa: literally "the second and the half". n is a sun letter, so al- assimilates again.

sentences.trap: Three sun letters in four words, and every one of them changes the spelling of al-. The build reads al-thāniya and ath-thāniya as different words, so the assimilation is not optional.
sentences.sound: ath-THĀ-ni-ya wan-NIṢF — the wa runs into the article and the whole thing is one phrase.

variations.cue: Half past five
variations.changed: another hour, same half

variations.display: nadhhab fī as-sāʿa ath-thāniya wa an-niṣf
variations.cue: We'll go at half past two
variations.changed: the time inside a plan

variations.cue: Quarter past two
variations.changed: the quarter instead of the half

mistake.why: th and n are sun letters: ath-thāniya, an-niṣf. Writing al- unassimilated gives the index two words nobody meant.

sentences.usage: The commonest time anyone arranges anything for, in Arabic as in every other language in this repo.
sentences.mnemonic: Sun letters swallow the l, and the build is watching.

words.note: The ordinal for four. r is a sun letter, so the article assimilates and the r is held long.
Built from the same three letters as ar-rābiʿa — r, b, ʿ — which is Arabic showing its roots. Four, fourth, quarter: one family, three shapes.

sentences.trap: ar-rābiʿa and ar-rubʿ share a root and are not interchangeable. Noticing the family helps the memory and does not help the grammar.
sentences.sound: ar-RĀ-bi-ʿa war-RUBʿ, with the ʿayn ending both words and the r doubled at the start of each.

variations.cue: Quarter past two
variations.changed: a different hour

variations.cue: We'll go at four o'clock
variations.changed: on the hour, with no quarter

variations.cue: Half past four
variations.changed: the half instead of the quarter

mistake.why: The ordinal agrees with as-sāʿa, which is feminine: ar-rābiʿa. The quarter does not, because it is its own noun.

sentences.usage: Quarter past is arranged; quarter to needs a word this course does not teach until it can be given a comparative note of its own.
sentences.mnemonic: One root, three shapes: four, fourth, quarter.

sentences.cue: Do you have an appointment on Friday?

words.note: The arranged time itself, and the word a plan ends up being called. The ʿayn is in the middle and must be sounded.
Named for the gathering, and the week's day of rest across the Arab world. j is a moon letter, so the l of al- is written and said.

sentences.trap: yawm goes in front of the day: yawm al-jumʿa. English says "on Friday" and Arabic names the day as a day.
sentences.sound: MAW-ʿid, with the aw as in "how". al-JUM-ʿa, with the ʿayn between the m and the a.

variations.cue: Do you have an appointment on Saturday?
variations.changed: the feminine address and another day

variations.cue: I have an appointment at five o'clock
variations.changed: the time rather than the day

variations.cue: I have an appointment on Saturday
variations.changed: the answer, with another day

mistake.why: The day takes yawm in front of it: yawm al-jumʿa. Without it the phrase reads as "Friday's appointment".

sentences.usage: Checking whether someone is free before proposing anything. It is the polite order of business.
sentences.mnemonic: Name the day as a day.

words.note: An adjective, so it agrees with the SPEAKER: muwāfiqa from a woman. The same law as āsif in M1 and shabʿān in M5.

sentences.trap: The plan is stated in the present and means the future. Arabic lets ghadan carry the tense, exactly as M6 of the level below let sa- do it — and here neither is needed.
sentences.sound: mu-WĀ-fiq, stressed on the long ā in the middle.

variations.cue: Agreed, we'll go tomorrow (a woman speaking)
variations.changed: a woman agreeing, so the adjective moves

variations.cue: Agreed, we'll go at five o'clock
variations.changed: sa- making the future explicit

variations.cue: Fine, agreed
variations.changed: M10's ṭayyib from the level below, in front

mistake.display: muwāfiqa, nadhhab ghadan (said by a man)
mistake.why: A man says muwāfiq. The agreement is his, so the adjective is his too.

sentences.usage: Sealing a plan. In business the fuller muwāfiq ʿalā dhālika exists; among people arranging a Friday, this is what is said.
sentences.mnemonic: Agreement is an adjective, and it belongs to whoever agrees.

words.note: s is a sun letter, so al- assimilates: as-sabt. The word is the same root as the Hebrew sabbath and the day it names is the working week's start in much of the region.

sentences.trap: The bare present, asked as a question, IS the suggestion. No extra word is needed — hal and the na- prefix do all of it.
sentences.sound: as-SABT, with the s held long and the final t fully released.

variations.cue: Shall we go on Friday?
variations.changed: the other day

variations.display: hal nadhhab ilā as-sūq yawm as-sabt?
variations.script: هل نذهب إلى السوق يوم السبت؟
variations.cue: Shall we go to the market on Saturday?
variations.changed: a destination as well as a day

variations.display: nadhhab yawm as-sabt, in shāʾ allāh
variations.script: نذهب يوم السبت، إن شاء الله
variations.cue: We'll go on Saturday, God willing
variations.changed: stated rather than asked, with the marker the next sentence explains

mistake.why: yawm goes in front of the day, as in S06: yawm as-sabt.

sentences.usage: The shortest suggestion in the module, and among friends the commonest.
sentences.mnemonic: hal plus we is a suggestion already.

words.note: M10's row from the level below, closing a plan rather than describing a thing. Its range covers OK, fine, all right and very well.

sentences.trap: Nothing new. Both halves are the learner's already, and putting them together is what ends a conversation about a plan.
sentences.sound: ṬAY-yib, with the y doubled and the ṭ emphatic.

variations.cue: Fine, see you on Saturday
variations.changed: the day named as you leave

variations.cue: Agreed, see you
variations.changed: S07's word in front instead

variations.cue: Fine, thank you very much
variations.changed: M1's thanks closing it instead

mistake.why: The phrase is frozen: ilā al-liqāʾ. Nothing is added to the end of it.

sentences.usage: The last line of the exchange. In Arabic the goodbye is always about the next meeting rather than this parting.
sentences.mnemonic: Goodbye in Arabic looks forward, not back.

sentences.display: in shāʾ allāh, nadhhab yawm al-aḥad
sentences.script: إن شاء الله، نذهب يوم الأحد
sentences.cue: God willing, we'll go on Sunday
sentences.literal: If wills God, we-go day the-Sunday

words.note: Named for the number one, because it is the week's first day. The hamza is written in the script and not in the romanization, since it is word-initial.

sentences.trap: in shāʾ allāh marks a future AND softens a refusal, and only the tone tells them apart. A plan sealed with it alone is not sealed, which is a fact about the language rather than about anyone's sincerity.
sentences.sound: in-SHĀʾ-al-LĀH, run together as one word in speech.

variations.cue: God willing, we'll go tomorrow
variations.changed: a nearer time

variations.display: nadhhab yawm al-aḥad, in shāʾ allāh
variations.script: نذهب يوم الأحد، إن شاء الله
variations.cue: We'll go on Sunday, God willing
variations.changed: the marker at the end, which is where it usually sits

variations.cue: Agreed, God willing
variations.changed: agreement and hedge in three words

mistake.display: in shāʾ allāh, sa-nadhhab yawm al-aḥad, muwāfiq
mistake.script: إن شاء الله، سنذهب يوم الأحد، موافق
mistake.why: One future marker is enough. sa- and in shāʾ allāh in the same sentence say the same thing twice.

sentences.usage: On the end of nearly every plan. Hearing it as a soft no is a skill; using it as one is a later lesson.
sentences.mnemonic: The plan and the doubt in the same four syllables.
